thread.title: Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou Arrest Slams Dow Jones; Two U.S. China Trade Scenarios

author: JED GRAHAM
title: Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou Arrest Slams Dow Jones; Two U.S. China Trade Scenarios

organizations.name: huawei cfo meng wanzhou arrest slams dow jones

text:
If past is prologue, a tweet from President Donald Trump will soon defuse the crisis sparked by the arrest of Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou. That's what happened after U.S. sanctions threatened to put Chinese communications gear maker ZTE out of business. Investor fears sparking Thursday's short-lived sell-off of the Dow Jones and broader stock market may not last. Yet the incident underscores the limits of any Trump trade deal on China tariffs.
X Apple ( AAPL ), Boeing ( BA ) and Caterpillar ( CAT ), whose close ties and hefty sales in China could be threatened by a failure of trade talks, were big Dow Jones losers Thursday. Trump has threatened to slap 10% tariffs on Apple iPhones produced in China. Apple stock fell 1.1%, Boeing stock 3.1% and Caterpillar 0.7% on the stock market today . The Dow Jones tumbled nearly 800 points intraday but closed down just 0.3%, or 79 points.
Will Trump Back Off Again? As with its initial punishment of ZTE, the Trump administration's first step against Huawei for violating U.S. sanctions on Iran was about the harshest option possible. Back in May, Trump pledged in a tweet to work with Chinese President Xi Jinping to get ZTE "back into business, fast," saying "too many jobs in China" were at stake. Similarly, Trump could seek the release of Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou and relatively lenient treatment of the cellphone and telecom equipment giant. Weng, who's also vice chair, is the daughter of Huawei's founder.
Yet the deepening distrust and geopolitical rivalry between the U.S. and China that led the Trump administration to lash out against both Chinese firms should tone down expectations for what a Trump-Xi China trade deal might achieve.

Please contact customer service CLOSE U.S. China Trade Rivalry Deep Any China trade truce is going to be narrow, with the U.S. still working to contain China via export controls, investment restrictions, World Trade Organization actions and trade agreements with allies. For example, Trump's update to Nafta, dubbed the U.S.-Canada-Mexico Agreement, gives the U.S. the right to pull out of the deal if either trading partner signs a China trade agreement.
For its part, the U.S. actions against key technology firms may leave China even more determined to pursue its state-funded Made in China 2025 ambitions to achieve global leadership in advanced technology industries.
The possibility of anything approaching a full resolution of the issues at the heart of the U.S.-China trade conflict — intellectual property rights, market openness, the skewed trade balance, cybertheft — seems even less likely today than it did yesterday, before the uproar of the Huawei arrest. China is calling the arrest a "human rights violation."
The Cold U.S. China Trade War Even with a trade agreement, the risk is rising that the global economy — especially high-tech sectors — will become divided between spheres of influence in a technological U.S.-China cold war . The U.S. wants to keep China's Huawei out of 5G next-generation mobile networks, citing security risks. China, through funding Belt and Road infrastructure projects in Asia, the Middle East and Africa, is working to expand its sphere of influence.
Given the geopolitical rivalry that shows no sign of diminishing, here are the two most likely scenarios for the future of the world's most important economic relationship:
The U.S. China Breakup: Two Scenarios The first scenario would be a trial separation, eventually leading to a divorce. This could include a retreat from tariffs in the near term and would be much less negative for the stock market and global economy.
The second scenario is a quick divorce, involving escalating China trade war tariffs, reprisals and significant disruption for the global economy and financial markets.
Despite the dust-up over Huawei, the first scenario still seems somewhat more likely because neither Trump nor Xi want to see a global recession. China is still building its advanced industries and isn't ready for a divorce. Trump, despite being "a Tariff Man," doesn't want to see the Dow or his presidential approval rating take a sustained nose-dive.
